transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-24
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Alvarez (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood CSM), Raj Patel (CTO, Nimbus), Maya Chen (Head of ML), Erik Johansen (Security), Lena Ortiz (Cloud Ops)

Summary:
Quick discovery to validate networking requirements for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood inference. Customer needs EU-only data residency, strict egress controls, prefer VPC peering but open to PrivateLink, interested in latency targets for customer chat flows. Discussed options: hosted + VPC endpoints, Dedicated with private control plane, or full Private (VPC + on-prem).

Topics:
- VPC peering vs PrivateLink/Transit Gateway
- Private endpoints and IP allowlist / egress
- Region constraints (EU-West1 preference)
- KMS/HSM / key control and audit logs
- SLA/uptime expectations and fallbacks
- Ramp/pilot and benchmarking plan

Action items (recap at end of transcript).

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Alvarez: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, Daniel our SE is here to go into the networking stuff.
[00:15] Raj Patel: Hey all, Raj here. Quick ask from my side, we need EU-only residency, all inference traffic and logs must stay in eu-west-1 and no egress to US. That's a hard req.
[00:28] Daniel Park: Totally understood. We have Private deployments that can fully run in your VPC in the eu-west-1 region, and our control plane can either be private or we can do a customer-managed control plane depending on the package.
[00:42] Maya Chen: When you say "control plane", can you clarify. We are concerned about metadata and audit logs leaving the VPC.
[00:50] Daniel Park: Yeah, so two patterns. With Redwood Private we can deploy a private control plane into your VPC (or a connected VPC) so telemetry and logs are retained in your network. Alternative is Dedicated where we provide a dedicated cluster but the control plane still talks to our managed services -- that's trickier for strict data residency.
[01:08] Lena Ortiz: Is there an option to use a PrivateLink endpoint instead of peering? Our infra team prefers minimal peering relationships.
[01:16] Daniel Park: PrivateLink is supported for certain flows, it exposes a private endpoint in your VPC without peering, but depends on traffic patterns. For high-throughput inference we usually see better throughput with peering or Transit Gateway to avoid NAT throughput limits.
[01:34] Erik Johansen: NAT is a no-go for us if it means egress through the internet. We also need to lock down outbound IPs for compliance scanner allowlists.
[01:43] Sofia Alvarez: Understood. We can provide a short list of egress IP ranges that our nodes will use when communicating to necessary Redwood services, and in a Private deployment those egress flows generally don't leave your VPC -- it's more about control plane integrations.
[01:58] Raj Patel: You mentioned KMS earlier, we need to use our KMS and HSM for key management -- full BYOK.
[02:06] Daniel Park: We support customer KMS integration; for Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/H-S-M via your VPC connectivity. Note sometimes our managed Key material for hosted models is separate, but for Private we can wire it into your KMS.
[02:21] Maya Chen: A lot of this is familiar, but let's talk latency. Our chat product needs sub-150ms tail latency at 1k QPS during business hours. Is that realistic with a private deployment?
[02:33] Daniel Park: Sub-150ms for tail is tight depending on model and sequence length, but with pinned model versions, optimized kernels and local GPU pools it's achievable. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated reserved pools with autoscaling and pinning to the EU region. Private gives you isolation but depends on the cluster sizing. We should run a benchmark with your payloads.
[02:52] Raj Patel: For fallback, if capacity is constrained do you have fallbacks to other regions or model variants? But again, region is a hard constraint so fallback has to be EU-only.
[03:05] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, our routing policies can be restricted to EU regions only; fallback can be to lighter model variants within the same region. We'll document that.
[03:15] Lena Ortiz: On peering -- if we peer to Redwood's VPC, that means cross-account peering in our cloud, correct? We are also evaluating Transit Gateway centralization.
[03:26] Daniel Park: Correct, cross-account VPC peering is the typical setup for low-latency high-throughput. Transit Gateway works well at scale if you already have a TGW and want central egress policies; PrivateLink is more managed but can be limited for large bulk data. There are trade-offs.
[03:42] Erik Johansen: How do you handle audit logs and access logs? We need immutable logs for at least 1 year and integration into our Splunk/SIEM.
[03:51] Hannah Lee: We can stream audit logs to your S3 bucket or CloudWatch in eu-west-1 and you can hook your SIEM to that. For Private we can keep the logging entirely within your account. There are edge cases with third-party observability addons but we'll scope those.
[04:06] Raj Patel: Is there any part of the control plane that still calls home to Redwood for updates? Patching?
[04:14] Daniel Park: Good question. For the managed control plane we do have update channels that connect to Redwood to pull patches; for air-gapped or fully private we provide an update package you can pull from an approved mirror or we can run a managed patch window under contract. We'll include the exact behavior in the security docs.
[04:31] Maya Chen: We heard about KV cache optimizations -- is that cached inside their infrastructure or in our VPC? Concern is caching of prompts and PII.
[04:43] Daniel Park: KV cache lives with the serving runtime. In a Private deployment it is in your VPC and under your tenancy so cached tokens do not cross out. In Dedicated hosted variants some cache metadata may be in our infra; we'll highlight which pieces are customer-resident.
[04:57] Raj Patel: What about network port requirements and firewall rules? Our infra team will need an exact list.
[05:05] Sofia Alvarez: We'll send a network playbook with ports, protocols, and CIDR ranges. That will include peering setup steps, required SGs, and PrivateLink endpoints if used.
[05:16] Lena Ortiz: Can you also include an example CloudFormation/Terraform snippet for peering? That speeds up our ops review.
[05:22] Daniel Park: Yep, we have Terraform snippets for peering, PrivateLink and TGW attachments; we'll attach those.
[05:30] Erik Johansen: SLAs -- we need an uptime commitment for production, and penalities? What's typical for Dedicated vs Private?
[05:39] Sofia Alvarez: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency tiers; Private deployments can be covered under an enterprise contract with custom SLAs. We'll propose standard terms and we can negotiate escalation paths and credit structures.
[05:52] Raj Patel: Cost -- is Dedicated more cost-effective than Private? We're trying to balance TCO vs the compliance needs.
[05:59] Sofia Alvarez: Generally Dedicated (Redwood-managed infra but reserved for you) is cheaper than a full Private (where you host VPC and possibly control plane), but Private gives you more control which can increase ops cost. We'll share a comparison worksheet with ballpark numbers for GPU types and hourly burn.
[06:15] Maya Chen: For the pilot, we want a small cluster, maybe a 2-node GPU pool in eu-west-1 and run a set of 1k concurrent sim requests for 48 hours. Can you support that?
[06:25] Daniel Park: Absolutely. We'll build a benchmark plan -- sample payloads, sequence lengths, expected tokenization, and we'll run both latency and throughput tests. We'll share the script and results.
[06:36] Raj Patel: Any compliance certifications you have that map directly to finance requirements? SOC2 was mentioned earlier.
[06:43] Hannah Lee: We can provide SOC2 Type 2, ISO 27001 summaries, and data handling policies. For Private we can also provide audit log exports and evidence for controls.
[06:55] Lena Ortiz: One other nit -- we have a strict list of allowed external dependencies; can Redwood run inside our service perimeter without access to other external services?
[07:05] Daniel Park: Yes for Private we can keep traffic internal. Some optional integrations (like telemetry or optional ML ops integrations) may need egress but are opt-in. We'll show a diagram for minimal footprint.
[07:20] Raj Patel: Ok, let's talk about identity. We use SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We need RBAC integration.
[07:29] Sofia Alvarez: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for user management; RBAC can be configured at role level. For Private deployments we can connect to your IdP in your network.
[07:42] Maya Chen: How are service-to-service creds managed? We prefer short-lived tokens and mutual TLS where possible.
[07:48] Daniel Park: We can do mTLS within the cluster and support short-lived credentials via your vault/KMS. We'll map options in the security doc.
[07:58] Raj Patel: Anything about model governance -- we need ability to pin model versions and do controlled rollouts.
[08:05] Daniel Park: Yes, pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policies are standard. We can integrate your evals to trigger regression alerts.
[08:15] (brief cross talk)
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: Back to peering -- if we do cross-account peering, what's the typical rotation for shared route tables and who owns them?
[08:28] Daniel Park: Typically the customer owns the route table; we provide the peering attachment and the route to the Redwood VPC prefix. If you use TGW, then attachments differ. We'll provide sample IAM/Terraform as requested.
[08:40] Raj Patel: Do you support multi-AZ by default? For high availability we need nodes across at least two AZs in eu-west-1.
[08:47] Daniel Park: Yes, multi-AZ is supported and recommended for HA. We'll show recommended AZ spread and instance types.
[08:58] Maya Chen: On the data side, do you purge cached prompts and logs on-demand? We may need to remove specific records.
[09:06] Hannah Lee: We support data deletion requests and can purge caches; for Private deployments that's easier because the data sits in your environment. We'll document retention policies and deletion procedures.
[09:18] Raj Patel: Are there any quotas or limits on model size or sequence length for Private?
[09:25] Daniel Park: There's practical limits based on GPU mem and kernel availability; we support large sequence lengths with chunking and KV cache strategies. For very long contexts we might recommend a different model family. We'll run sample runs with your workloads.
[09:38] (screen share note) Daniel shared a slide with network topologies: peering vs PrivateLink vs TGW
[09:48] Daniel Park: On the slide you can see the throughput and operational tradeoffs. Peering = low-latency but cross-account. PrivateLink = managed endpoint but potential throughput limits. TGW = good for centralized networks.
[10:00] Raj Patel: For authentication between our services and the model endpoints, do you provide mTLS client certs or IAM-role-based auth?
[10:09] Daniel Park: Both are supported. Within AWS you can use IAM-based auth or mutual TLS for service-to-service. We also support token-based auth for SDKs with short-lived tokens.
[10:21] Maya Chen: Ok, one more on telemetry -- do you stream request/response logs? That's PII risk so we need to be careful.
[10:30] Hannah Lee: We stream metadata and optional request traces; payload-level logs are opt-in and can be disabled. For Private deployments payloads can be kept local and never forwarded.
[10:44] Raj Patel: Great. Let's talk timeline -- we'd like a pilot in 3-4 weeks and production in 3-4 months. Is that feasible?
[10:52] Sofia Alvarez: That matches our usual cadence. Pilot in 3-4 weeks is reasonable assuming we get IP ranges and test payloads in the next week. Production timeline depends on contracting and any custom SLA terms.
[11:03] Lena Ortiz: Any blockers from our side? We'll need legal to review the contract and security team will want the SOC2 artifacts.
[11:11] Sofia Alvarez: We'll send the security pack. Legal review usually takes 2-3 weeks on your side, we can parallelize.
[11:21] (longer discussion on pricing models, not transcribed verbatim)
[20:10] Daniel Park: Going back to the benchmarking plan -- for the pilot we'll do two phases: latency-focused runs for tail percentiles and throughput runs for sustained QPS. We'll include warmup, KV cache scenarios, and sequence length distribution.
[20:27] Maya Chen: Please include tokenization details -- our payloads are highly variable.
[20:32] Daniel Park: Yup. We'll instrument token count histograms.
[28:44] Erik Johansen: Security follow-up: can you provide proof-of-cleanroom testing and any third-party pentest reports?
[28:50] Hannah Lee: We have summary pentest reports and can share redacted findings; for deeper asks we can SSO into a secure doc exchange.
[29:05] Raj Patel: Last question: if we choose Dedicated rather than Private, can we still get peering and the same KMS options?
[29:15] Daniel Park: Dedicated can peer into your VPC for low-latency connectivity and we support customer KMS for encryption-at-rest metadata in many cases, but the control plane behavior is slightly different. We'll list exact differences in the architecture doc.
[29:30] Sofia Alvarez: Ok, next steps recap -- I'll send security docs, Terraform snippets, and the pricing worksheet. Daniel will prepare the benchmark plan and sample scripts. Erik will send the IP ranges. Maya will share payload specs.
[29:47] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Also please add a diagram showing a fully private control plane flow.
[29:54] Daniel Park: Will do.
[30:00] (wrap up, thanks)
[47:30] Sofia Alvarez: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule the deep-dive next week.

End of transcript.
